title: The Loneliness of Buying Too Many Things
text:
Maybe you remember them: the credit-card offers—so congratulatory, so seductive—that pour into graduating college seniors’ mailboxes. To the unwary, they seem to promise free money. In practice, they can often lead to debt. This is what happens to Becky Bloomwood, the protagonist of the chick-lit classic Confessions of a Shopaholic , by the British writer Sophie Kinsella. The novel opens with a bank offering Becky an extended overdraft of £2,000 for her first two years in the workforce. Mere pages later, the two years are up, and Becky, now a financial journalist with a serious shopping habit, owes the bank thousands of pounds.

 Confessions of a Shopaholic came out in the United States 25 years ago, and certain aspects of the book haven’t aged at all: Becky’s chatty warmth is as enjoyable as ever, and the debt she racks up will likely be relatable to as many readers now as in the early aughts. But the details and texture of her shopping—physical credit cards swiped, department stores wandered through—are so unlike the reality of today’s consumerism, with its smartphones and scrolling, that the novel is almost a time capsule.

 Becky’s eagerness, her longing, and her bubbly charisma made Confessions of a Shopaholic a hit when it was published—surprising, perhaps, for a comic novel about a woman with a shopping addiction. Although it received hardly any critical attention, it was, along with Helen Fielding’s Bridget Jones’s Diary and Lauren Weisberger’s The Devil Wears Prada , core to one of the most popular genres of its time.

 Yet, unlike some of its peers, Confessions of a Shopaholic is a fundamentally solitary, even lonely, book. Becky’s focus on shopping crowds out other characters. Perhaps this is why the novel’s film adaptation hasn’t endured; contrast it with those of Bridget Jones’s Diary and The Devil Wears Prada , which have surpassed the books themselves. Fielding’s and Weinberger’s novels revolve around friendship, romance, or careers that involve collaborating with others—all relationships that are easy to dramatize on-screen. But the central relationship in Confessions of a Shopaholic is Becky’s connection to, and yearning for, material things. She’s at her most emotional when shopping, which, with very few exceptions, she does alone. As a result, the book’s most captivating sections are internal monologues directed at objects that can’t want Becky back. The adaptation, starring Isla Fisher, does its best to create new versions of these moments—in one scene, a mannequin talks to Becky—but it doesn’t capture the book’s real drama, which is inside its heroine’s head.

 If Confessions of a Shopaholic had been written in 2026, Becky would be more solitary still—so alone that the novel might not work at all. Kinsella, who died late last year, was gifted at buoying readers along through the sheer power of voice, but even she might not have been able to make a charming, compelling read out of a woman scrolling through pages and pages of buyable things on her phone. In fact, reading the novel today is at once a reminder of how much shopping has changed and a grim preview of what was to come: As consumers, at least, we’re all as alone as Becky Bloomwood now.

 Confessions of a Shopaholic does have characters other than its heroine. Kinsella introduces readers to Becky’s parents; her supremely posh roommate, Suze; a fellow financial journalist, Elly, who shares Becky’s interest in fashion; the bank and credit-card-account managers who pursue her; and, naturally, her enemy turned love interest, a communications mogul and Eligible Bachelor named Luke Brandon. Yet these characters don’t speak all that much, and, though it’s clear to the reader that she needs some intervention, the only ones who challenge her are calling to collect debt.

 That the people around Becky never help her is part of the novel’s plot, not a failure of its writing. Kinsella demonstrates that Becky learned her acquisitiveness from her mother, and also gives enough (very funny) detail about Suze’s upper-class background that readers will understand why she’s too clueless to help her friend rein in her wild spending. In fact, Suze’s wealth lets her enable Becky: She’s rich enough to give her roommate breaks from the rent. The only person who can meaningfully confront Becky about her shopping habit is Becky herself, but for all her anxiety about overextending herself financially, that’s not something she intends to do. “If everyone could just wear new clothes every day,” Becky muses, “I reckon depression wouldn’t exist anymore”—and readers know she believes this is true.

 [ Read: A better way of buying—and wanting—things ] 

 In 2026, a shopaholic like Becky could blow their earnings on the internet. Becky spends her money—and her time—out in the world. She tells the reader, “There’s a thrill about walking into a shop—any shop—which you can’t beat.” The novel’s tensest interactions, the ones most loaded with desire and expectation, take place between Becky and store employees who don’t know her name. It’s these women (and they’re always women) who see her most vulnerable self.

 In an early scene, Becky begs an employee at a luxury store to hold a marked-down scarf behind the register for her; she’s left her credit card at work and will have to go get it. Over the course of this conversation, her face “flames red”; she speaks “quickly,” “desperately,” and “beseechingly.” When the shopgirl eventually agrees to reserve the scarf until that evening, Becky is overcome with “a combination of relief and adrenaline.” Kinsella’s prose here makes exceedingly clear that Becky doesn’t just have a cute shopping problem. It’s an addiction that—even if Becky’s friends and family don’t clock it—is on public display.

 Kinsella doesn’t blame her heroine for her predicament; Confessions of a Shopaholic , for all its effervescence, is a straightforward critique of consumer culture. Becky is a decidedly unreflective character: She does not have—or seem inclined to develop—the self-awareness to examine the world of deals and sales and reward points that she inhabits. But the novel knows from the start that these bargains are traps, such as the supposedly no-strings-attached overdraft offer that gets Becky in trouble. Throughout the book, various moments of visceral longing—Becky says of a pair of £90 zebra-print jeans: “If you were in Gucci, you’d be paying at least £500. Oh God, I want them, I want them”—make obvious that Becky, living amid all the shops of London, is effectively a gambler in a city of slot machines. She’s surrounded by temptation, and there’s always some way not to say no.

 [ Read: ] A close-up look at the waste of modern life 

 But this is chick lit, not Uncut Gems . Confessions of a Shopaholic still ends happily, with Becky landing a rich boyfriend and a lucrative job. With her new salary, she’ll be able to pay off her overdraft and keep shopping—and Kinsella dangles the promise that soon, Becky will have a wealthy husband to foot her bills. In short, Becky’s problems are solved, yet she remains on the isolated treadmill of her compulsions: want new things, buy new things, repeat.

 A contemporary Becky would arguably have an even easier time continuing to shop, and a harder time resisting. She’d have a smartphone in her pocket, overflowing with tempting sale offers and the promise of buy-now-pay-later services that encourage people—especially women, as my colleague Annie Joy Williams has reported —to spend even further beyond their means than credit cards already do.

 Most likely, it would also be full of posts and messages from influencers who recommend products to their followers in casual, effusive tones—not unlike the voice that Kinsella gives Becky. In a sense, the Shopaholic movie got something right with that talking mannequin: Like the TikTokers and Substackers making money from their followers’ clicks and purchases, the mannequin allows Becky to feel like she’s shopping with a friend when, really, she’s alone.

 Seen in this light, the loneliness of Confessions of a Shopaholic feels more straightforward than it might today. None of the shopgirls Becky encounters pretends to care about her. Of course, their detachment—snootiness, sometimes—is a chosen persona, but their engagement with Becky is fundamentally honest: They’re selling; she’s buying. No one is promising, or projecting, any other sort of connection. Reading the novel today is a reminder that the pseudosocial nature of a lot of present-day shopping is a trap far more sophisticated than the customer-reward points that get Becky to overspend on moisturizer. Becky’s addiction separates her from other people, but, 25 years later, she’d risk adding a potentially more unsettling layer to her isolation—mistaking consumerism for a version of friendship. I doubt even Kinsella could have made anything but the darkest comedy out of that.
